signals.title: 3 Ways to Boost MoE Inference on NVIDIA DGX Spark | NVIDIA Technical Blog
signals.excerpt:
Generating tokens faster starts with identifying what limits inference performance. In the batch-size-1 evaluation of Ling-3.0-flash from Inclusion AI on NVIDIA DGX Spark, profiling showed that decoding was memory-bound: reading model weights drove execution time. Two operations stood out—the mixture-of-experts (MoE) computation and the output-layer projection that produces scores across the model’s vocabulary.

Those findings pointed to two ways to improve performance: reduce the weight traffic in each decode step and generate more tokens per verification round. This post examines three techniques that address those costs:

- Humming MXFP4 MoE kernels to improve execution of the routed-expert computation.
- Online FP8 quantization of the output layer, or LM head, to reduce its weight-read volume.
- Multi-token prediction (MTP) speculative decoding with NEXTN to draft and verify multiple tokens together.

This post explains how each optimization works, measures its effect, and examines an integration issue that can make the combined configuration slower than the baseline. Ling-3.0-flash serves as the implementation example, with code and deployment instructions in the Ling cookbook.

...

## Optimization 2: Online FP8 LM head quantization

In the checkpoint, the LM head is stored in BF16 and listed in modules_to_not_convert, so it is not quantized during loading. Its vocabulary GEMM is 157,184 × 2,560, and the entire weight block must be read for each generated token. Under a bandwidth bottleneck, it is therefore a high-value target for compression.

The optimization applies a dynamic FP8 quantization configuration only when constructing the LM head. The rest of the model continues to load with the checkpoint’s FP8/MXFP4 configuration. Moving the LM-head weights from BF16 to FP8 halves the read volume for this layer. The configuration is enabled with SGLANG_ENABLE_FP8_LM_HEAD=1.

This setting is mutually exclusive with the baseline –enable-fp32-lm-head option, which outputs logits in FP32 and uses a slower vocabulary-GEMM path.

| Configuration | TPOT | Decode throughput | Relative to baseline |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Baseline | 27.71 ms | 36.09 tok/s | — |
| + Humming MoE backend | 25.35 ms | 39.45 tok/s | +9.3% |
| + Online FP8 LM head | 22.76 ms | 43.94 tok/s | +21.7% |

Table 2. Cumulative effects of Humming and online FP8 LM-head quantization on NVIDIA DGX Spark, using a synthetic workload with 32K input tokens, 2K output tokens, and batch size 1. Adding FP8 increases decode throughput by 11.4% over Humming alone

...

## Conclusion

Across the full GSM8K evaluation, the three optimizations increased decode throughput by 42.5%, reduced mean end-to-end latency by 24.5%, and produced no statistically detectable accuracy change. Their mechanisms do not overlap: Humming and the FP8 LM head reduce the cost of each step, while MTP reduces the number of steps, so the techniques can be combined.

Stacking, however, is not automatic. Each optimization worked independently, but enabling all three required the draft model to share the full LM-head module. Otherwise, the system silently degrades to a configuration slower than the unoptimized baseline. During deployment, validate that every optimization is active at startup; this is more reliable than inferring configuration state from later performance numbers.

signals.title: Introducing GPT-6.1 Terra | OpenAI
signals.excerpt:
Introducing GPT-6.1 Terra | OpenAI
# GPT-6.1 Terra
## Delivering fast and capable computer use at scale
We’re introducing **GPT-6.1 Terra**, a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. A significant step up from GPT‑5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos.
Terra continues to advance the cost-intelligence frontier across our model families, providing a new balance of speed, capability, and cost. Its standard API prices are 50% lower than those of GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol, making it practical for developers to automate high-volume work, like reading incoming invoices and entering their details into accounting software. In ChatGPT Work and Codex, your plan goes further with GPT-6.1 Terra—the same usage allowance covers more tasks than with GPT‑5.6 Terra and substantially more than with GPT‑6.1 Sol or GPT‑6 Astra.
## From visual understanding to action
We measured GPT-6.1 Terra’s computer-use capabilities on **Agents’ Last Exam,** a benchmark of professional tasks that includes turning architectural drawings into a 3D model and reviewing an animated film shot by shot to create a time-coded log for a restoration team. At medium reasoning effort, GPT-6.1 Terra scores 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra at about one-third the cost. It even performs on par with GPT-6 Astra at only one-tenth its price per token. At max effort, Terra is over three times as token efficient as Claude Opus 5.5, and one-fourth its price per token, resulting in a \~9x lower cost per task. Terra is also much quicker, completing tasks **over three times faster** than both GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol.
On **MMMU-Pro**, a benchmark of visual reasoning, GPT-6.1 Terra outperforms GPT-5.6 Terra at every reasoning setting. It even nearly matches the scores of our most capable frontier model, GPT-6 Astra, and GPT-6.1 Sol at much lower cost.
**OSWorld 2.1** tests how well AI agents use desktop apps to complete multistep tasks, such as building a 3D model from a technical drawing. At medium reasoning effort, GPT-6.1 Terra surpasses GPT-5.6 Terra’s best score at a fraction of the cost per task.
## A significant step up on factuality and coding
This year, we’ve invested heavily in reducing hallucinations and factual errors produced by our models. On our internal benchmark of error-inducing prompts, the error rate at low reasoning effort fell from 53.6% with GPT-5.6 Terra to 16.7% with GPT-6.1 Terra, a drop of nearly 37 percentage points. At maximum effort, the error rate fell by 18 percentage points to 4.3%, nearly matching the rates for GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol.
GPT-6.1 Terra marks a substantial improvement over GPT-5.6 Terra for software engineering. **Terminal-Bench 4.0** tests how well coding agents solve problems from the command line, such as fixing a webpage whose layout shifts as it loads. At maximum reasoning effort, GPT‑6.1 Terra solves 50.3% of tasks, more than double GPT‑5.6 Terra’s published score of 21.5%. For the most complex coding tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra remain the better choice.
**Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1** tests how well agents use code to carry out scientific research tasks, such as tracking cell divisions in a time-lapse video. At max reasoning, GPT-6.1 Terra surpasses GPT-6.1 Sol at lower cost, coming within five points of Opus 5.5 at less than one-fifth the estimated cost.
## Safety and alignment
As we make powerful AI more efficient and accessible, we continue training, testing, and refining our safeguards. GPT‑6.1 Terra meets the Critical threshold in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, and maintains the protections developed for GPT‑6 Astra.
GPT-6.1 Terra brings with it the alignment improvements of the GPT-6 series. According to our evaluations, GPT-6.1 Terra is more likely to stay within scope and honestly disclose limitations and potential blockers to the user compared to GPT-5.6 Terra. In our prompt-injection tests, GPT-6.1 Terra also showed strong resistance to malicious instructions designed to divert it from the user’s task. More detail is available in the system card⁠(opens in a new window).
## Pricing and availability
Starting today, GPT-6.1 Terra is available to all Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex. Developers can also access it through the OpenAI API as `gpt-6.1-terra`.
Standard API pricing is $1 per million input tokens, $0.05 per million cached input tokens, and $5 per million output tokens.

signals.title: AI agents on a short leash: PipesHub searches company knowledge | heise online
signals.excerpt:
### Permission-Aware Search

PipesHub is an open-source, self-hosted alternative to commercial enterprise search services such as Glean. The system, developed on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license, is aimed at companies and development teams that want to make internal data sources searchable or provide them as context for large language models and AI agents without sending data to third-party cloud environments. The software connects to existing systems through more than 50 connectors and inherits their access permissions (permission-aware search). Anyone who isn’t allowed to see a document in Google Drive or a ticket in Jira also won’t receive information from it through PipesHub or connected AI assistants. The system includes citations in its answers, down to individual text passages.

Technically, the platform combines a vector database (Qdrant) for similarity searches with a graph database — Neo4j or ArangoDB by default — as well as MongoDB. With this knowledge graph approach, PipesHub captures not only similar text passages but also structural relationships between documents, users and systems. For language models, the project says on its website it follows a “Bring Your Own Model” approach: Administrators can connect APIs from providers such as OpenAI or Anthropic, or run local models through Ollama. External tools such as Claude Code or Cursor can access the knowledge context through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) or SDKs for Python, TypeScript and Go.

signals.title: Uncertainty-aware offline reinforcement learning for LLM inference serving with heterogeneous SLOs | Scientific Reports
signals.excerpt:
Uncertainty-aware offline reinforcement learning for LLM inference serving with heterogeneous SLOs | Scientific Reports
* Article
* Open access
* Published: 26 October 2026
# Uncertainty-aware offline reinforcement learning for LLM inference serving with heterogeneous SLOs
* Enmiao Feng 1,
* Gaike Wang 2,
* Pengfei Li 1,
* Yinuo Wang ORCID: orcid.org/0009-0004-3927-0742 3 &
* …
* Shan Huang 4
## Abstract
Large language model (LLM) inference workloads are bursty, have output lengths that are unknown at arrival, expose two resource-distinct phases (prefill and decode), and serve requests carrying heterogeneous service-level objectives (SLOs) on time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-per-output-token (TPOT). Prevailing schedulers rely on static heuristics that cannot adapt to this uncertainty, while online reinforcement learning (RL) is unsafe and sample-inefficient in production. We present URSA, an uncertainty-aware, risk-sensitive scheduler trained *entirely offline*, without interacting with a live serving system, on scheduling transitions generated by replaying historical request traces under existing heuristic schedulers. URSA (i) predicts a calibrated *distribution* over each request’s output length and derived key–value (KV) cache footprint rather than a point estimate; (ii) encodes the joint state of the waiting queue, heterogeneous GPU instances, and KV occupancy as a request–instance heterogeneous graph processed by a graph neural network; (iii) learns a dispatch policy with conservative, distributional offline RL whose reward jointly optimizes SLO attainment, goodput, and KV-overflow risk; and (iv) reserves memory at a class-dependent high quantile of the predicted footprint to bound out-of-memory events. Across the BurstGPT, Azure LLM inference, and Alibaba GPU-cluster traces, URSA raises overall SLO attainment from \\(71.3\\%\\) (FCFS) and \\(84.1\\%\\) (learning-to-rank) to \\(90.4\\%\\), cuts P99 TTFT by up to \\(3.3\\times \\), and reduces recompute/eviction events below \\(1\\%\\), approaching an oracle that knows true lengths. We analyze limitations, robustness to prediction error, and transfer to other scheduling domains.

# PyTorch 2.15 Release Blog

Source: https://pytorch.org/blog/pytorch-2-15-release-blog/

Last updated: 2026-10-28

---

We are excited to announce the release of PyTorch® 2.15 (release notes)!

The PyTorch 2.15 release features the following changes:

- Rewritten NCCL backend becomes the default, with a flight recorder that dumps on hangs and `TORCH_DIST_USE_NCCL2=0` or `nccl-legacy` as rollback paths
- One-sided transports for torch.distributed, with a NIXL backend and CUDA-graph-capturable transfers
- **FSDP2 and pipelining gain finer memory and communication control,**with fp32 for precision-sensitive parameters, CUDA-graph-captured gradient accumulation, and gradient reduction overlapped with compute 
-   Faster 4-bit (NVFP4) LLM decoding on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs through fewer, better-overlapped kernel launches in NVGEMM
- Apple Silicon gains FP8 and faster decode, with `float8_e4m3fn` and `_scaled_mm`, a new grouped_mm with a decode fast path (1.32–1.34x tokens/s on MoE decode), and public `torch.mps.Stream` APIs
- Broader platform support with FlyDSL kernels on AMD gfx950, Tensor Data Mover support for gfx1250 (MI450), ROCm 10.0 wheels, simpler SYCL kernel authoring and multi-GPU profiling on Intel GPUs, CUDA 13.2 as the default wheel with CUDA 13.4 alongside it, and torch.compile on Python 3.15

signals.title: We're open-sourcing DevBox, our autonomous engineering harness - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
We're open-sourcing DevBox, our autonomous engineering harness - DEV Community
Posted on Oct 28 • Originally published at rudderstack.com
# We're open-sourcing DevBox, our autonomous engineering harness
*Originally published on the RudderStack blog.*
DevBox is an open source engineering harness you hand a task to the way you would a teammate. It works out which repositories need to change, makes the change, tests it, reviews its own diff, and opens a draft pull request. It's MIT-licensed, runs on your own infrastructure, and talks to your own model endpoint. The code is at github.com/rudderlabs/devbox.
We've been running DevBox across our own engineering organization since April. Since then:
* **1,500+** pull requests opened
* **80%** merge rate
* **66** repositories touched
## The backlog that never moves
Every engineering organization carries work that's clearly worth doing and never worth prioritizing. An API client that needs one more field mapped. A test with a timeout too tight for CI. A dependency pinned three minor versions back. Documentation that drifted from the code six weeks ago.
None of it competes with roadmap work, so none of it gets scheduled. It accumulates, and the cost shows up somewhere else: the flaky test everyone reruns, the integration gap that becomes a support ticket, the upgrade that turns into a week of work because it never got the hour it needed.
The work is understood. Most of these tickets could be written precisely in about two minutes. They sit because no engineer has a free afternoon.
We built DevBox for that work, and we're releasing it under the MIT license.
## What DevBox does about it
DevBox works from Linear. Assign it an issue, or mention it on one. What comes back is a draft pull request that DevBox has already tested and reviewed itself. You review that pull request on GitHub and leave your comments there, or you reply in the Linear session instead. Either way it pushes new commits to the same branch.
*Figure 1. You hand over a ticket and get back a draft pull request. Everything in between happens on its own, and your comments start another round on the same branch.*
The scope is deliberately narrow. DevBox handles short to medium tasks that are already well understood. It doesn't replace an engineer designing a complex feature, and we don't run it that way. Human review and steering are part of the design. Follow-up rounds handle corrections: a missed edge case, a test to add, a naming convention to respect. They aren't for redesigning the approach.
Each agent writes down what it's doing, in the Linear session as it goes: the decision it took and the alternative it passed over, the correction a reviewer gave it, the mistake it made and what the right answer turned out to be. The decisions explain why the pull request looks the way it does, which is usually a reviewer's first question. A mistake that keeps coming back points to a gap in your documentation, or to code worth restructuring so the mistake can't happen.
*Figure 2. What an agent writes down as it works. Illustrative entries, not from a real run.*
After implementation, a distillation stage decides which of those observations are worth keeping and files them by domain into the repository's knowledge files: architecture, conventions, patterns, entry points, the stack. Those files are committed in the same pull request as the code change, so new knowledge arrives for review next to the work that produced it.
When DevBox learns something wrong, you see it in the diff and correct it, the same way you'd correct a misleading comment or a stale README.
*Figure 3. What DevBox learns arrives as a diff. Distilled notes land in the repository's knowledge files, in the same pull request as the code, and your review comments feed the next task.*
## It follows your conventions
The objection we hear most about coding agents is that they write code the way an outsider would, ignoring conventions a team spent years settling.
DevBox reads its instructions from the repositories it works on. Build commands, test commands, naming rules, the patterns you want and the ones you've banned live in files like `AGENTS.md` at the repository root, next to the code, reviewed like everything else. DevBox can only follow conventions you've written down.
Most of those conventions live in skills, self-contained packages of instructions and expected workflows that sit in the repository alongside the code. A skill describes how one kind of work is done here, such as how a migration is written, or which checks run before a change counts as finished.
DevBox runs each stage as a separate agent and hands each one the skills it needs before the work starts.
*Figure 4. Each agent gets the conventions and skills of the repository it works on. Repository names are examples.*
## How it works
Assigning a Linear issue to DevBox calls a webhook on its control plane. The control plane asks OpenSandbox for an isolated environment for that one task, starts it, and watches it.
From there DevBox is on its own. The harness runs inside the sandbox, carries out the task, and reports progress back to the control plane, which posts it to the Linear issue as it goes. At the end it opens a pull request. Nobody has to intervene before that point, and in practice people rarely do.
Leaving DevBox alone like that is only reasonable because the sandbox is sealed. Everything it sends out goes through iron-proxy, which adds the real credentials the sandbox never holds, and refuses any host that isn't on the allowlist.
Once the pull request exists, the control plane watches for your response: a review or comment on the pull request, a failed CI run, or a message in the Linear session. Any of those starts another round of work on the same branch.
*Figure 5. One sandbox per task, and one route out. Every outbound call passes through the proxy, so the hosts an agent can reach are set in configuration.*
The control plane is a Bun service with Postgres, sandboxes come from OpenSandbox (containers on a laptop, pods on a cluster), the agents are built on DeepAgents, and iron-proxy handles egress. The whole thing installs from a Helm chart.
Inside the sandbox the work moves through fixed stages, and each stage is its own agent. The first reads the repositories and your conventions. The next decides which repositories to change and writes a plan, and another agent argues with that plan before a line of code is written. Implementation runs one agent per repository. Then up to six reviewers go over the diff at the same time, each looking for a different class of problem, and a fix pass either resolves what they found or records why it disagreed.
Each agent can run on its own model and reasoning effort. Review can run on a stronger model at high effort while the early reading stages run cheaply, so cost and quality are set per stage instead of once for the whole pipeline.
*Figure 6. The task pipeline. Each stage runs as its own agent, with its own model and effort. The plan is reviewed before any code changes, and the review and fix loop repeats up to a configured limit before anything is committed.*
## Why it's safe to point at your private repositories
Most teams hesitate before giving an autonomous process a token with write access to their source code. Five properties of the design address that.
* Your credentials never enter the sandbox. It receives dummy values for the GitHub token and the model key, and iron-proxy substitutes the real ones as requests leave.
* The sandbox can only reach hosts you allow. iron-proxy is its only route out and its only name resolver, and anything not on the allowlist is refused, so nothing in the sandbox can send your source code to a host that isn't on the list.
* Writes are limited to the repositories you list. Anything outside that list is refused at the proxy rather than discouraged in a prompt.
* DevBox only takes instruction from people you designate, because anyone who can comment on a pull request could otherwise try to steer it. You name the trusted organizations and users, and if you name nobody it reads no pull request discussion at all.
* Each task gets its own environment. Tasks don't share a workspace, so one can't corrupt another's branch or state.
*Figure 7. The sandbox holds nothing worth stealing. Real credentials are added at the proxy, and only for the hosts you allow.*
For production, run DevBox on Kubernetes, where each task is its own pod and the egress rules are enforced by network policy. You can go further and give sandboxes a runtime class, so each one is a Kata Containers virtual machine instead of a container sharing the host kernel. The chart ships a production example that does that, on dedicated nodes. The Docker Compose path exists so you can try DevBox on a laptop in an afternoon. It isn't the shape to run a team on.
*Figure 8. From a laptop to a VM per task. The chart's production example runs sandboxes as Kata VMs on dedicated nodes.*
## What it has done for us
We run DevBox across our own engineering organization. Since April it has opened 1,500+ pull requests across 66 repositories, and 80% of the pull requests it took to a decision were merged. The rest were closed after a person read the change and judged it not worth taking.
The rate rose every month: 72% in August, 79% in September, 91% in October. Our read is that two things changed. DevBox got more capable, and we got better at briefing it.
*Figure 9. Monthly merge rate: merged pull requests divided by those merged or closed in the month. October runs to the 26th.*
*Figure 10. Pull requests DevBox opened from August to October 2026, by type of change.*
A third of it is small features. They're small in a specific way: one more field in a mapping, an audit for an API version change, a configuration flag behind a safe default. Work that can be specified precisely and is never urgent enough to schedule.
One recent example: a new customer hit a bug in one of our integrations in their first weeks with us. DevBox had a pull request open 21 minutes after an engineer approved the work, and the fix was live for every customer that afternoon.
The pull request that relicensed DevBox under MIT, ahead of this release, was opened by DevBox.
## Where it doesn't work well
DevBox fails in predictable ways, and the failures cluster into three kinds.
* Vague tickets produce vague changes. A one-line issue with no detail gets a change that misses the point. What works is a spec. An engineer refines the requirements into the issue description before delegating, and that moves the outcome more than any configuration we've tried.
* Tribal knowledge is invisible to it. When a workflow lives in people's heads instead of in the code, DevBox can't follow it and will confidently do something else. Write it down in the repository, or teach it through follow-up comments on the pull request, which the distillation stage then records for later tasks.
* The harness needs an image built for your stack: the toolchain, the versions, and the dependency trees that are slow to resolve from scratch. Build that image before you judge the results.
These are the problems a new engineer hits in their first week, and they respond to the same fixes.
If your team requires a review before merge, someone still reviews every pull request DevBox opens. Those pull requests are easier to review. Each covers one task, follows the conventions you wrote down, and comes out of the same plan-and-review process every time. Short, predictable pull requests are cheaper to read than long, surprising ones.
## Run it yourself
DevBox is MIT-licensed and self-hosted. You bring your own model endpoint and key, so your code and your prompts go to a provider you already have a relationship with. It works with OpenAI-compatible endpoints and with Anthropic's API.
Getting started takes one configuration file listing the repositories DevBox may touch and your model endpoint, then a single command to bring the stack up. The first build takes about ten minutes. Connect it to Linear and GitHub, delegate an issue in Linear, and watch the draft pull request arrive.
The source code, quickstart, and Kubernetes guide are at github.com/rudderlabs/devbox. Pick one ticket from the backlog that never moves and hand it to DevBox.

# DeepSeek-V4 Flash RL on AMD Instinct MI308X GPUs with an AITER-Backed RL Stack
## Contents
# DeepSeek-V4 Flash RL on AMD Instinct MI308X GPUs with an AITER-Backed RL Stack #
October 28, 2026 by Danyang Zhang, Oliver Wu, Yongsheng Xu, Sijie Li, Lei Wu, Jun Kang Chow, Giuseppe Grossi, Indira Vats, Shengnan Xu, Hongxia Yang, Lingpeng Jin, Carlus Huang, Jacky Zhao, Zhong Cai, Peng Sun, Emad Barsoum.
6 min read. | 1576 total words.
Ecosystems and Partners
Reinforcement Learning, AI/ML, Training, LLM
AI, Systems
We demonstrate end-to-end DeepSeek-V4 Flash reinforcement learning with an AITER-backed AMD RL stack on 24 AMD Instinct MI308X GPUs. Our test covers the complete workflow on three MI308X OAM nodes—not only inference or an isolated training step, but long-context FP8 rollout, BF16 MoE actor training, online RDMA weight updates, evaluation, and checkpoint recovery. Training and inference run as disaggregated services: two MI308X nodes host a BF16 actor that preserves the numerical stability required by gradient computation and optimizer updates, while a dedicated third MI308X node hosts an FP8 rollout engine whose smaller per-parameter footprint leaves more GPU memory available for KV cache and longer generated sequences. Ray places and coordinates both GPU groups. This experiment demonstrates one tested three-node configuration for running both rollout inference and RL training on MI308X GPUs.
This post reports the first 75 optimizer steps of a long-context GRPO run on three eight-GPU AMD Instinct MI308X nodes. The AITER-backed workflow combines distributed orchestration, rollout correction, routing replay, weight transfer, evaluation, and checkpoint recovery around an FP8 rollout engine and a BF16 actor.
## Key Takeaways #
* DeepSeek-V4 Flash RL was tested on MI308X. The complete 24-GPU, three-node AITER-backed workflow ran on AMD Instinct MI308X OAM systems.
* The MI308X deployment supports disaggregated training and inference. Two MI308X nodes run a 16-worker Megatron actor through an AMD-native training backend with AITER-backed kernels; a third MI308X node runs an eight-way tensor-parallel vLLM rollout server.
* The first 75 optimizer steps maintained stable generation throughput. Mean rollout throughput was 311 generated tokens/s, with a measured range of 287–331 generated tokens/s.[1]
* Online reward improved over the run. Mean reward accuracy increased from 45.3% in Steps 1–25 to 53.2% in Steps 26–50 and 59.2% in Steps 51–75.[1]
* Held-out AIME-2024 accuracy improved. Accuracy over eight generations per problem increased from 30.0% at Step 1 to 49.2% at Step 75.[1]
## DeepSeek-V4 Flash in the AITER-Backed RL Stack #
According to the DeepSeek-V4 technical report, DeepSeek-V4 Flash is a 284-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with roughly 13 billion active parameters per token. The model supports a one-million-token context window and has 43 decoder layers with a hidden size of 4,096 and a 129,280-token vocabulary. The run reported here limits the model context and total sequence length to 16,384 tokens. Every decoder block contains one shared expert and 256 routed experts, with six routed experts activated per token. The first three MoE layers use deterministic hash routing; later layers use the learned router.
The attention schedule interleaves three layer types. The first two layers use dense sliding-window attention (SWA) over 128 tokens. The remaining 41 layers alternate between 21 Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA, or C4) layers and 20 Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA, or C128) layers. CSA pools the sequence at 4:1 and selects the top 512 compressed entries; HCA pools at 128:1 and attends densely over the compressed sequence. Both retain the 128-token local branch, preserving recent-token resolution alongside long-context access.
Each attention module has 64 query heads reading a shared 512-dimensional key/value latent. Queries use a rank-1,024 low-rank path shared with the sparse indexer, while the output projection is divided into eight groups with 1,024-dimensional bottlenecks. These shapes are important to the specialized ROCm attention and projection kernels used by the AMD-native training backend.
DeepSeek-V4 Flash replaces a conventional residual connection with manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC) over four parallel residual streams. A pre-mixer collapses the streams into the tensor consumed by each sub-layer; a post-mixer expands the result back into the four-stream state. The rollout and actor engines must preserve this mapping, the hybrid-attention schedule, and expert assignments even though they execute different kernels and numerical formats. In this workflow, vLLM generates trajectories from an FP8 representation, while Megatron-LM uses the AMD-native DeepSeek-V4 backend and AITER-backed training kernels to score and update the policy in BF16.
Figure 1 summarizes the model components and routing path that the rollout and actor engines must preserve.
Figure 1. Simplified DeepSeek-V4 Flash block showing four-stream mHC mixing, the SWA/CSA/HCA layer schedule, and top-6 routing over 256 experts. Adapted from the DeepSeek-V4 technical report.
### Why MI308X Support Matters #
This experiment shows that the tested MI308X configuration—together with the ROCm, AITER, and vLLM ecosystem around it—can support an RL training pipeline: distributed BF16 actor training with Megatron, FP8 rollout generation with vLLM, online RDMA weight updates, evaluation, and checkpoint recovery. The result is specific to the three-node configuration and software versions reported in the test configuration below.
DeepSeek-V4 Flash stresses several MI308X subsystems at once: large-capacity HBM for a 284B-class MoE policy, high-throughput FP8 execution for rollout, multi-node collectives for TP/PP/EP actor training, and RDMA for repeated online policy updates. Passing only a model-load or single-step test would not exercise this complete path.
Our 75-step result exercises this integrated workflow across all three nodes. The actor topology, optimizer offload, activation recomputation, vLLM memory headroom, AITER kernel path, and RCCL transport settings were selected specifically to make long-context DeepSeek-V4 Flash RL practical on MI308X. The MI308X actor uses TP4/PP4/EP4, while rollout uses TP8 on a dedicated node.
The AMD-native training backend supplies the DeepSeek-V4 Megatron layer specification, architecture modules, ROCm compatibility paths, quantization lifecycle abstractions, and AITER-backed operators. The surrounding RL orchestration layer provides inference integration, rollout correction, reward processing, online weight updates, evaluation, and recovery.
## The AITER-Backed Execution Flow #
Figure 2 shows how the three-node deployment separates rollout from actor training while coordinating online policy updates.
Figure 2. The disaggregated DeepSeek-V4 Flash RL workflow spans three MI308X nodes. An AMD-native backend connects the Megatron actor to the DeepSeek-V4 model specification and AITER-backed training kernels. The actor and rollout engines use independent parallel layouts and exchange updated policy weights through RCCL RDMA.
The RL orchestration layer manages the lifecycle around those engines:
1. sample prompts from DAPO-Math-17K;
2. generate eight responses per prompt with vLLM;
3. score the responses with the math reward;
4. rescore generated tokens with the Megatron actor;
5. form group-relative advantages;
6. apply token-level rollout importance-sampling correction;
7. update the BF16 actor;
8. transfer and quantize the new policy for the FP8 rollout engine;
9. periodically evaluate on AIME-2024 and save distributed checkpoints.
### 1. Ray Separates Training and Rollout #
The run uses three nodes with eight GPUs each. Ray pins 16 actor workers to two nodes and eight rollout workers to the third node. This separation lets the Megatron actor use a memory-oriented parallel layout while vLLM uses a throughput-oriented tensor-parallel layout. On the training side, the AMD-native backend provides the DeepSeek-V4 Megatron layer specification and connects AITER-backed kernels for model operations on MI308X.
The actor uses:
* tensor parallelism: 4;
* pipeline parallelism: 4;
* expert parallelism: 4;
* expert tensor parallelism: 1;
* sequence parallelism and full activation recomputation;
* 11 layers in the first pipeline stage and 10 in the last;
* distributed Adam with full optimizer-state CPU offload;
* BF16 optimizer moments with 256 MiB streamed-Adam chunks.
The rollout engine uses:
* vLLM AsyncLLM with tensor parallelism 8;
* FP8 per-block weights and FP8 E4M3 KV cache;
* AITER kernels where supported;
* a 16,384-token model context and 4,096-token response cap;
* up to 8,192 batched tokens and 48 concurrent sequences;
* 90% GPU-memory utilization.
The 90% memory target reserves GPU memory for online policy updates while retaining KV-cache capacity for long generated sequences.
### 2. GRPO Keeps the Policy Loop Explicit #
Each optimizer step samples 32 prompts and generates eight responses per prompt, producing a global batch of 256 trajectories. The RL orchestration layer evaluates the responses with the DAPO math reward, computes group-relative advantages, and aggregates the policy loss with sequence-mean/token-mean semantics.
The policy update uses a learning rate of `1e-6`, a GRPO clipping ratio of `0.2`, and an upper clipping ratio of `0.28`. No explicit KL reward penalty is enabled in this experiment.
Because rollout and training use different numerical representations, the workflow applies token-level importance-sampling correction. The correction clamps the train-versus-rollout ratio at 2.0 and applies it directly to the per-token GRPO loss. For the MoE path, hard-assignment R3 replay preserves the recorded rollout routing decisions during actor rescoring.
### 3. RDMA Updates a Live FP8 Rollout Engine #
After each actor update, the workflow transfers the updated policy through an RCCL-backed RDMA group. The actor remains BF16, while the rollout engine prepares the FP8 representation before the next generation cycle. Rollout resumes only after the distributed update has completed.
### 4. Checkpoints Make Long Runs Recoverable #
The orchestration layer saves a distributed checkpoint every 25 optimizer steps and retains the latest two checkpoints. The actor checkpoint includes model, optimizer, and scheduler state across the Megatron topology. Resume restores the actor before rebuilding the RDMA group and reloading the rollout workers.
## Seventy-Five-Step Results #

signals.title: Cerebras Maps 3-Trillion-Parameter Kimi K3 Across 59 Wafer Chips | AI.info
signals.excerpt:
Cerebras’ October 22 deployment guide describes how it maps the roughly 3-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model across 59 WSE-3T wafers, keeping model weights on-chip while requests move through a pipeline. The company presents the design as an example of serving models larger than any one wafer’s memory, not as an independently measured benchmark report.

...

## Why Kimi K3 takes 59 wafers

A WSE-3T wafer has 44 GB of on-chip memory, while Kimi K3’s weights alone require terabytes at ordinary precision. Cerebras works through an illustrative configuration using 4-bit weight quantization, an 8-bit key-value cache and an assumed average request length of 256,000 tokens. Under those assumptions, the company estimates each of the model’s 93 layers at about 16 GB.

The layer mix determines how Cerebras distributes the model. Kimi K3 has 69 linear-attention layers and 24 dense, or full-attention, layers. Cerebras assigns two linear layers to a wafer, using 32 GB of its 44 GB, but reserves one wafer for each dense layer because dense attention stores keys and values for tokens in active requests.

That arithmetic yields 35 wafers for the linear layers and 24 for the dense layers: 59 altogether. The remaining memory on dense-layer wafers holds KV cache. The estimate depends on the stated quantization and request-length assumptions; it is not a universal wafer count for every model or serving configuration.

...

## Weights stay put as activations move

Cerebras describes execution as a pipeline. Its compiler maps layers to wafer regions, then the runtime routes tokens between stages. The post says activations—the intermediate results passed between layers—travel over RDMA over Ethernet, with roughly two microseconds per hop. The model weights generally remain where they are placed, avoiding the need to move them between wafers for each request.

In the guide’s simplified example, one wafer runs layers 1 and 2, then sends its activations to a second wafer running layers 3 and 4. Production deployments use finer-grained stages, the company says. That distinction matters: the two-layer illustration explains the principle, but does not specify the exact stage layout of a production Kimi K3 deployment.
